newsitem.title: RWANDA: U.S., U.N. at odds on Rwandan refugee numbers. [CORRECTED 10:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S., U.N. at odds on Rwandan refugee numbers. [CORRECTED 10:30 GMT]

text.p: The U.S. army said on Saturday its week-long assessment showed 202,000 refugees remained in eastern Zaire and many might decide not to return to Rwanda.

U.S. army Major-General Edwin Smith, leader of the U.S. team, denied the military was in any "contest for credibility" over numbers. But 202,000 was a third the number of refugees estimated by the U.N. refugee agency as still trapped in Zaire.
The Rwandan government said it supported the U.S. figures and that a multinational force for Zaire was unnecessary in the wake of the return to Rwanda since November 15 of 600,000 refugees.

Smith said he did not want to influence talks currently underway in Stuttgart on any multinational force. But some aid officials put the U.S. estimate in the context of a U.S. aim to avoid intervention.

"We've identified right now approximately 202,000 refugees (in east Zaire) and 600,000 that have moved back into Rwanda," said army Major Marty Schweitzer, briefing aid workers and journalists on results of the investigation since November 15.
The estimates were obtained from photographs taken by U.S. surveillance aircraft flying over eastern Zaire until Friday.

Schweitzer said "clearly there is a delta" between the U.S. estimates of 802,000 refugees in eastern Zaire and Rwanda now and the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) figure of 1.23 million in east Zaire before the November 15 exodus.
UNHCR officials said they believed up to 600,000 refugees remained in eastern Zaire, having scatteed to escape fighting.

Schweitzer said the shortfall might be the result of UNHCR overestimation and substantial refugee movements (Corrects explanation) before a revolt by Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels that triggered the mass return.
U.S. officials, who declined to be identified, said they did not trust UNHCR's figure of 1.23 million as no accurate census had been taken of refugees in Zaire before the crisis.
Schweitzer said the U.S. team concluded that the remaining 202,000 would probably not return to Rwanda at the same flood rate as the 600,000 that had gone home in one week.
"Substantial parts (of the 202,000) may choose not to return at all," said Schweitzer, who added the return home of the 600,000 was "a success story" for Rwanda's government and aid agencies.

An aid official, who declined to be identified, said it was "an insult to intelligence" for the U.S. military to say many would not choose to return when many refugees were being herded by Rwandan Hutu Interhamwe militiamen and former Hutu troops.
"Even if the U.S. numbers are right, the analysis, obtained from planes overhead and without even setting foot in eastern Zaire, shows little understanding of this crisis," he added.
General Smith said surveillance systems had limitations but were highly accurate over time and the U.S. team could not have missed a mass concentration of refugees in the area surveyed.
UNHCR officials said there were innumerable small camps of up to 15,000 refugees and U.S. planes flying a corridor 100 km (60 miles) wide would have missed many refugees who had fled west.
General Smith said the U.S. assessment could not tell the difference between Zaireans displaced by the fighting, put by U.S. officials at 200,000, and Rwandan or Burundian refugees.

Schweitzer said the largest single refugee mass was between 150,000 and 200,000 west of Lake Kivu heading north. He said they stopped on Thursday on the western side of the Mutumba mountains but were believed to have resumed moving on Friday.

U.N. officials quoted a witness who visited the mass on Tuesday as saying they were in a temporary camp at Numbi and former Rwandan troops and Interahamwe militiamen had set up checkpoints on the approaches and felled trees to block roads.

The U.S. team estimated the main mass included up to 100,000 former Rwandan troops and their families heading north and west. The former Rwandan troops and Interahamwe militiamen led the genocide in Rwanda in 1994 and then fled to east Zaire.
"UNHCR always exaggerates its figures. We believe the U.S. estimates are correct," said Claude Dusaidi, a senior adviser to Rwandan military strongman Vice-President Paul Kagame.
"We don't need a force, we need food and medicine for the vast majority of refugees who have returned," he told Reuters.
